title: Different Types of Redundancy and Their Effect on Learning and Cognitive Load https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bjep.12592
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton's page covers a study by Albers, Trypke, Stebner, Wirth, and Plass that separates two things often lumped together as 'redundancy' in multimedia learning: content redundancy (the same information given in different formats, such as animation plus narration) and modal redundancy (the same information repeated within the same mode, such as animation, narration, and on-screen text all at once). In a 2x2 within-subject design with university students, content redundancy improved learning and reduced cognitive load, while modal redundancy did the opposite -- harming learning and increasing cognitive load. This directly challenges the blanket assumption that 'all redundancy is bad,' a common shorthand drawn from cognitive load theory. Barton draws out the practical distinction for teachers designing multimedia materials: repeating information across different modes (animation and narration together) tends to help, but stacking the same information across too many modes at once (animation, narration, and matching on-screen text) tends to overload working memory and hurt learning.
points: Content redundancy (the same information across different modes, e.g. animation plus narration) improves learning and reduces cognitive load.
Modal redundancy (the same information repeated within the same mode, e.g. animation, narration, and matching text together) harms learning and increases cognitive load.
This challenges the common blanket assumption from cognitive load theory that all redundancy is bad for learning.
The ideal level of content overlap likely depends on task difficulty and learners' prior knowledge, with the expertise-reversal effect in play.
quotes: The results suggest that modal redundancy harms learning and increases cognitive load. The results also suggest that content redundancy enhances learning and decreases cognitive load

Favor content redundancy over modal redundancy. When designing multimedia learning materials, prioritize repeating information across different modes (e.g., animation and narration) instead of presenting the same information multiple times within the same mode (e.g., animation, narration, and text)

Consider the difficulty of the task and students' prior knowledge. The ideal level of content overlap might vary depending on the complexity of the learning task and the expertise level of the learners
Avoid overloading students with too much information. While repetition is helpful, overwhelming students with excessive input can hinder learning
A study using a 2x2 within-subject design with university students found that content redundancy improved learning and reduced cognitive load, while modal redundancy had the opposite effect
